content:
Quick answer: A Mediterranean-style pattern is a practical healthy-eating option, not a cure for arthritis. Choose vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, nuts and small amounts of unsaturated oils. If you eat fish, the NHS advises at least two portions weekly, including one oily. NICE says there is no strong evidence that dietary changes benefit rheumatoid arthritis itself. Keep prescribed treatment.

This guide distinguishes general healthy-eating advice from evidence about arthritis symptoms. NICE recommendations apply to particular conditions; they do not certify a commercial diet, supplement or meal plan.

Search for "anti-inflammatory diet" and you will find long lists of superfoods, banned foods and expensive supplements. It is easy to come away thinking that if you just ate the right things, your arthritis would go away. That is not what the evidence shows, and it can leave people feeling guilty or spending money they do not need to.

Food choices can help you meet nutritional needs and manage weight where appropriate. They do not establish that inflammation is controlled or joint damage is prevented. You do not need special products, and ongoing symptoms are not a personal failure to eat well.

What does "anti-inflammatory diet" actually mean?

There is no official, agreed definition. When researchers and dietitians talk about an anti-inflammatory way of eating, they usually mean a pattern that looks a lot like the traditional Mediterranean diet:

  • lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds
  • wholegrain starchy foods rather than refined ones
  • olive oil or rapeseed oil as the main fats
  • fish, especially oily fish, regularly
  • moderate amounts of dairy, eggs and poultry
  • less red and processed meat, sugary food and drink, and highly processed snacks

That pattern fits closely with the NHS Eatwell Guide, which is the UK's official model of a healthy balanced diet. So an anti-inflammatory diet is not a special or extreme diet. It is mostly healthy eating, with a lean towards plants, fish and unsaturated fats.

What the evidence says

Rheumatoid arthritis

NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100, recommendation 1.8.8) says that adults with RA who want to experiment with their diet should be told there is no strong evidence that their arthritis will benefit. It adds that they could be encouraged to follow the principles of a Mediterranean diet: more bread, fruit, vegetables and fish, less meat, and replacing butter and cheese with products based on vegetable and plant oils.

An older 2009 Cochrane review found uncertain effects from the small dietary trials available then. It is not the latest research. A 2025 systematic review reported promising results for some dietary interventions alongside medicines, but the studies differed too much to combine their results and the authors called for better long-term trials. This supports further research, not a promise that a particular food pattern will control your disease.

The British Dietetic Association's November 2026 advice is positive about Mediterranean-style or plant-based patterns and recommends discussing changes with a rheumatologist and dietitian. That professional advice and NICE's more cautious statement should be read together. Do not stop a DMARD or judge disease control from a change in pain alone. These RA findings cannot automatically be transferred to psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis or gout.

Osteoarthritis

NICE NG226, recommendation 1.3.5, addresses weight management for people with osteoarthritis who are living with overweight or obesity. Any weight loss is likely to help pain, function and quality of life; losing 10% of body weight is likely to be better than 5%. This is not a requirement to lose weight before receiving care, and it is not advice for someone who is underweight or losing weight unintentionally. Discuss a suitable goal and support with your team. The BDA's current osteoarthritis advice discusses possible dietary-pattern benefits, but does not establish a food that rebuilds cartilage. See our healthy weight guide for practical support.

The honest summary

ClaimWhat the evidence supports
A Mediterranean-style diet is a sensible choice with arthritisNICE allows encouragement of Mediterranean principles in RA, while stating there is no strong evidence that dietary changes benefit the arthritis itself.
Diet can replace arthritis medicinesNo. Keep prescribed treatment and discuss changes with your treating team.
Specific "superfoods" can switch off inflammationNo particular food is established as a cure or a substitute for disease-modifying treatment.
Cutting out whole food groups helps most peopleNot supported; it can make it harder to get enough nutrients
Losing excess weight helps osteoarthritisYes. NICE says it improves pain and function

Why it still matters if it is not a cure

A varied diet supplies protein, fibre, vitamins and minerals. The aim is adequate nutrition and a pattern you can sustain, rather than a guaranteed change in pain, fatigue or blood-test results.

  • Food variety: use several food groups rather than replacing meals with a single juice, powder or supplement.
  • Weight: if weight loss is appropriate, ask for a realistic plan that still meets nutritional needs. Do not use crash diets or prolonged fasting as an arthritis treatment.
  • Bones: dairy or suitable fortified alternatives provide calcium. Vitamin D advice is separate from claims about treating arthritis pain. Ask about bone health if you take steroids.
  • Medicine safety: eating well does not prevent every medicine side effect. Report problems and keep your prescribed monitoring appointments.
  • Persistent fatigue: do not assume food is the only cause. Speak to your healthcare team if tiredness or poor appetite continues.

Foods to eat more of

Food groupWhyEasy UK ideas
Vegetables and fruitFibre, vitamins and plant compounds. The NHS recommends at least 5 portions a day, about a third of what you eatFrozen peas, spinach, berries and mixed veg; tinned tomatoes; bagged salad; bananas and apples
WholegrainsFibre and starchy carbohydrate. The NHS suggests higher-fibre or wholegrain choices.Porridge oats, wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholewheat pasta, potatoes with skins
Beans, lentils and pulsesProtein and fibre, low in fatTinned chickpeas, baked beans (reduced sugar and salt), red lentils, frozen edamame
Oily fishLong-chain omega-3 fats (EPA and DHA). The NHS advises at least 2 portions of fish a week, 1 oilyTinned sardines, mackerel or pilchards; salmon fillets; kippers
Nuts and seedsUnsaturated fats; walnuts and flaxseed contain plant omega-3 (ALA)A small handful of unsalted nuts; ground flaxseed on porridge
Olive and rapeseed oilUnsaturated fats instead of butter and lardRapeseed oil for cooking, olive oil for dressings

If you eat fish, aim for at least two portions a week, including one oily, rather than treating two oily portions as a universal target. The NHS gives separate maximum limits for children and people who are pregnant, breastfeeding or may become pregnant. Fresh and canned tuna do not count as oily fish. If you avoid fish, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds can still be part of a varied diet; ask a dietitian about individual needs.

Foods to have less often

The NHS Eatwell Guide places foods high in fat, salt and sugar outside the main guide, to be eaten less often and in small amounts. For an anti-inflammatory pattern, it also makes sense to cut back on:

  • processed meats such as bacon, ham, sausages and salami
  • sugary drinks, sweets, cakes and biscuits
  • foods high in saturated fat, such as fatty meat, butter, ghee and pastry
  • salty snacks and ready meals (adults should have no more than 6g of salt a day)
  • Alcohol: if you drink, the general low-risk guideline is no more than 14 units a week, spread over at least three days. This is not a personal safe allowance with every medicine or medical condition. Ask your pharmacist or treating team what applies to you.

Do not routinely remove dairy, gluten or nightshade vegetables to treat arthritis. If symptoms seem linked to a food, discuss them with a dietitian or clinician before a restrictive diet. Our food-trigger guide is further reading, not proof that a food causes your symptoms. Gout has separate food and medicine considerations; do not assume every fish-rich meal plan suits someone with gout.

A sample anti-inflammatory day

This is an example, not a prescription. Portion sizes depend on your age, size, activity and goals, which is something a registered dietitian can help with.

MealExample
BreakfastPorridge made with milk or a fortified soya drink, topped with frozen berries and a spoonful of ground flaxseed
LunchWholemeal pitta with hummus, salad and tinned mackerel, plus an apple
SnackPlain yoghurt with a few walnuts, or carrot sticks and hummus
Evening mealChickpea and vegetable curry made with tinned tomatoes and spinach, served with brown rice
DrinksWater, tea or coffee; the NHS suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day

For more ideas, see our meal plans for arthritis and Mediterranean diet guide. These are optional examples, not individual prescriptions.

A check across your day or week

The NHS Eatwell Guide describes the overall balance across a day or even a week. You do not need to reproduce its proportions at every meal.

  1. Are fruit and vegetables varied, with at least five portions a day and just over a third of food overall?
  2. Is there a starchy food, ideally wholegrain or with the skin on?
  3. Is there a protein food, such as fish, beans, lentils, eggs, chicken or tofu?
  4. Is the fat mainly olive or rapeseed oil rather than butter or lard?
  5. Is there a source of calcium somewhere in the day, such as milk, yoghurt, cheese or a fortified alternative?

These checks concern a balanced diet. They do not measure inflammation or prove that your arthritis is responding. People with kidney disease, diabetes, food allergies, swallowing difficulties or other dietary needs may need a different plan.

Making it work when your joints hurt

Cooking from scratch can be hard when your hands or knees are painful, or when fatigue is bad. Healthy eating does not have to mean lots of chopping:

  • Use convenient options: frozen vegetables, tinned beans and microwave grains can reduce preparation. Compare labels for salt, sugar and other ingredients rather than assuming all packaged food is unsuitable.
  • Batch cook on good days. Make a big pot of soup, chilli or curry and freeze portions.
  • Buy pre-prepared. Ready-chopped vegetables, microwave rice pouches and pre-cooked lentils save effort.
  • Use tools. Jar openers, lightweight pans, a perching stool and good knives can help. An occupational therapist can advise.
  • Keep easy standbys. Wholemeal toast with sardines or baked beans is a quick, balanced meal.

What about supplements?

Many products are marketed as anti-inflammatory. The evidence for most is limited, and some can interact with arthritis medicines:

  • Fish oil: eating fish is not the same as taking a concentrated supplement. Some RA studies report symptom benefits, but this does not establish a universal dose, control of joint damage or a replacement for prescribed medicines. The BDA does not recommend omega-3 supplements routinely for the general population. Ask a pharmacist about the exact product, especially with blood thinners or other medicines.
  • Turmeric: a November 2026 Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence of little or no improvement in knee osteoarthritis pain, function or quality of life compared with placebo, and very uncertain harms. Concentrated turmeric products have also been linked with rare liver injury. Cooking-spice use is a different exposure. See our turmeric evidence and safety guide.
  • Folic acid and methotrexate: follow your prescribed folic acid plan. The NHS advises against adding products containing folic acid when you already take prescribed folic acid. It also says there is not enough information to establish the safety of other herbal remedies or supplements with methotrexate.
  • Vitamin D: the NHS advises adults and children over four to consider 10 micrograms daily in autumn and winter. Some people need it throughout the year. This is nutritional advice, not proof of an arthritis pain treatment. Follow individual medical advice and check before taking higher doses.

If you take warfarin, do not suddenly remove green vegetables or greatly increase them. NHS anticoagulant advice recommends a consistent intake of vitamin-K-rich foods and a check before major dietary changes. This specific food restriction does not usually apply to apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban. Product and medicine checks still matter. Our food, drink and arthritis medicines guide is further reading.

When to see a dietitian

A registered dietitian can give advice tailored to you. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral if:

  • you want to lose weight and have not managed on your own
  • you have lost weight without trying or have a poor appetite
  • you are thinking about cutting out food groups, such as dairy or gluten
  • you have another condition that affects your diet, such as diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease or gout
  • you are vegan or eat a very restricted diet

Dietitian is a protected professional title in the UK. You can check registration with the Health and Care Professions Council.

When to get medical help

Do not stop or change prescribed medicines because of a diet change. Ask your pharmacist or team before starting a supplement. Arrange a medical review for unexplained weight loss, poor appetite or persistent digestive symptoms.

A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without a fever. Joint infection must not be dismissed as a dietary trigger or an ordinary flare. In England, Scotland and Wales, ask for an urgent GP appointment or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service.

Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency, such as severe breathing difficulty, confusion or blue, pale or blotchy skin during a possible serious infection. See NHS sepsis advice. If you take an anticoagulant, get urgent advice about bleeding or a head injury; severe or unstoppable bleeding needs emergency help. See NHS anticoagulant safety advice.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a proven anti-inflammatory diet for arthritis?

No single eating plan is established as a cure or replacement for arthritis treatment. Mediterranean-style eating is a reasonable option for general health. NICE says there is no strong evidence that dietary experiments benefit rheumatoid arthritis itself, while allowing encouragement of Mediterranean principles.

How long does it take to notice a difference?

There is no reliable personal timetable for arthritis symptom improvement from changing diet. You may not notice a pain change. Keep your treatment and review plan, and ask for help if symptoms are worsening.

Do I need to cut out dairy, gluten or nightshades?

Do not routinely cut out these foods to treat arthritis. A diagnosed allergy, coeliac disease or another condition may change the advice. Discuss symptoms and testing with a clinician or dietitian before removing a whole food group.

Is the anti-inflammatory diet expensive?

It need not involve specialist products. Oats, beans, lentils, frozen vegetables and ordinary supermarket oils can be practical options. Choose foods you can afford and prepare, rather than treating a costly label as evidence of benefit.

Can I still eat red meat?

Yes, in moderation. The aim is to eat less red and processed meat and more fish, beans and pulses, not to ban foods completely.

Should I take anti-inflammatory supplements?

Most have limited evidence. If you want to try one, check with a pharmacist or doctor first, especially if you take warfarin, other anticoagulants, methotrexate or NSAIDs.

General information for adults in the UK, not individual dietary or medical advice. Ask a registered dietitian or your treating team about your own nutritional needs and medicines. This editorial revision has not had a fresh clinical review by Louis Maxwell.

key_takeaways: Diet is not a cure for arthritis or a replacement for prescribed treatment.
NICE distinguishes RA dietary uncertainty from OA weight-management advice.
NHS advice is at least two fish portions weekly, including one oily, with separate limits for some groups.
Check medicine interactions and seek tailored help before restrictive diets or supplements.
